quote: wie viel Schnittflächen müssen gelegt werden damit sich jede geschlosse- ne Fläche im so zerschnittenen Raume auf 0 zusammenziehn lässt.
english: How many cut surfaces must be laid so that every closed surface in the space thus cut can be contracted to 0?
topic: Defines a first and second genus (p_1, p_2) of a space by the number of cut surfaces needed so that every closed surface, respectively every closed curve, can be contracted to a point, raises the existence problem for algebraic configurations with a prescribed branching scheme (a generalisation of Riemann's existence theorem), and lists coloured relations between three functions U, V, W.

triage.modern_statement: For a 3-dimensional space (manifold) M, find the minimal number of cut surfaces needed so that every closed surface in the cut space bounds, meaning it can be shrunk to nothing. This is the Riemann–Betti 'connectivity number' in dimension 2. In modern terms it is the second Betti number b_2(M) = rank H_2(M), possibly up to the historical +1 convention. Hilbert's companion invariant, cutting until every closed curve contracts, corresponds to b_1. Read literally, 'contracted to a point' is a homotopy notion (π_2 / π_1). The cut-number formulation actually matches homology, and the two notions differ in general.
triage.answered_by: Enrico Betti, 1871 ('Sopra gli spazi di un numero qualunque di dimensioni'), generalised Riemann's cut-based connectivity to higher dimensions, giving numbers b_k. Heegaard (1898) showed that Betti's cut definitions had errors. Poincaré's 'Analysis Situs' (1895) and its supplements (1899 onward) put these numbers on a sound footing as homology Betti numbers and stated Poincaré duality (b_k = b_{n-k} for closed orientable n-manifolds). Later homology theory made them standard invariants.

evidence.claim: Betti published higher connectivity numbers in 1871, generalising Riemann's cut-based connectivity of surfaces.
Betti (1871) introduced connectivity numbers b_k, later called Betti numbers, for each dimension 1 ≤ k ≤ n of an n-manifold, generalising Riemann's analysis situs.
Heegaard found errors in Betti's proofs in 1898, and Poincaré in Analysis Situs defined Betti numbers via homology, with a corrected treatment after Heegaard's criticism.
Poincaré's 1895 Analysis Situs founded algebraic topology and its homologies and Betti numbers; supplements followed Heegaard's criticism.
Poincaré duality: for closed orientable n-manifolds, the k-th and (n−k)-th Betti numbers are equal (stated in 1893, 1895).

triage.why: Hilbert's p_1 and p_2 are Riemann–Betti connectivity numbers for surfaces and curves in a 3-dimensional space. Betti had already defined them in 1871, and Poincaré's homology theory (1895–1904) settled them rigorously. Today they are the standard Betti numbers, computable for any finite complex. So this is not an open problem and is not one of Hilbert's published problems. Confidence is medium for two reasons. First, the page cannot be dated against Poincaré's work. Second, the wording mixes contractibility, a homotopy notion, with cut counting, a homology notion, and these differ in general. If Hilbert meant π_2 literally, cut counts do not capture it; that subtlety was clarified by later homotopy theory (Hurewicz, 1930s), but no source I found ties it to this note.
